nodes.label: Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach, 9th ed., Chapter 2 Application Layer
nodes.author: J.F. Kurose and K.W. Ross
nodes.rationale: Pearson 2025 slides covering application-layer principles, HTTP, e-mail, DNS, video/CDNs, and socket programming. Copyright 1996-2025.

nodes.label: Application layer
nodes.rationale: Network apps run on end systems and communicate by messages. Network-core devices do not run user applications, which keeps app development at the edge.

nodes.label: Client-server paradigm
nodes.rationale: Server is always-on with a permanent IP, often in data centers for scaling. Clients may be intermittent, may have dynamic IPs, and do not talk directly to each other. Examples: HTTP, IMAP, FTP.

nodes.label: Peer-to-peer architecture
nodes.rationale: No always-on server; peers request and provide service. Self-scalability: new peers add capacity and demand. Intermittent connectivity and changing IPs make management complex. Example: BitTorrent.

nodes.label: BitTorrent
nodes.rationale: Named example of P2P file sharing and listed again in the chapter summary as the P2P protocol studied.

nodes.label: Socket
nodes.rationale: Door between the application process and the transport protocol. The app developer controls the process side; the OS controls transport below the socket. Two socket types: UDP datagrams and TCP byte streams.

nodes.label: Process addressing (IP address and port)
nodes.rationale: A host 32-bit IP address does not identify a process because many processes share a host. The identifier is IP address plus port. HTTP server port 80; mail server port 25. Example: gaia.cs.umass.edu at 128.119.245.12 port 80.

nodes.label: Application-layer protocol
nodes.rationale: Defines message types, syntax, semantics, and send/respond rules. Open protocols are specified in RFCs so anyone can interoperate (HTTP, SMTP). Proprietary protocols include Zoom.

nodes.label: TCP
nodes.rationale: Reliable transport, flow control, congestion control, and connection setup between processes. Does not provide timing, minimum throughput, or security. Used by FTP, SMTP, HTTP, and streaming via DASH.

nodes.label: UDP
nodes.rationale: Unreliable datagram transfer with no flow control, congestion control, timing, throughput guarantee, security, or connection setup. Chosen when those services are unnecessary. Also the substrate for QUIC and HTTP/3.

nodes.label: Transport Layer Security (TLS)
nodes.rationale: Vanilla TCP and UDP sockets send cleartext. TLS, implemented in the application layer via libraries that use TCP, adds encryption, data integrity, and endpoint authentication so cleartext written into the socket is encrypted on the wire.

nodes.label: HTTP
nodes.rationale: Web application-layer protocol. Browser client requests objects; Web server responds. Uses TCP, typically port 80. Stateless: the server keeps no memory of past requests because endpoint state is complex and can diverge after crashes. Request methods include GET, POST, HEAD, and PUT. Sample status codes: 200, 301, 400, 404, 505.

nodes.label: Non-persistent HTTP
nodes.rationale: At most one object per TCP connection, then the connection closes. Per-object time is 2 RTT plus file transmission. Multiple objects need multiple connections, plus OS overhead; browsers often open parallel TCP connections.

nodes.label: Persistent HTTP (HTTP/1.1)
nodes.rationale: Server leaves the TCP connection open so later objects skip a new handshake. Client can send the next request as soon as it sees a reference. As little as one RTT for all referenced objects, about half the non-persistent response time.

nodes.label: HTTP cookies
nodes.rationale: Because HTTP itself is stateless, sites keep user state with four pieces: Set-Cookie response header, Cookie request header, a browser cookie file, and a back-end database. Uses include authorization, carts, recommendations, and webmail sessions. First-party cookies track one chosen site; third-party cookies track across sites. Firefox and Safari disable third-party tracking by default.

nodes.label: Web cache (proxy server)
nodes.rationale: Satisfies requests without the origin server when the object is cached. Acts as server to the client and client to the origin. Cuts response time because the cache is closer, and cuts institutional access-link traffic. In the example, a 0.4 hit rate drops access-link utilization from 0.97 to about 0.58 and average delay to about 1.2 s, cheaper than upgrading a 1.54 Mbps link to 154 Mbps.

nodes.label: Conditional GET
nodes.rationale: Browser sends If-Modified-Since with the cached copy's date so the server can skip the object. Up-to-date cache yields 304 Not Modified; a newer object yields 200 OK with the body. Avoids transmission delay and network use.

nodes.label: HTTP/2
nodes.rationale: RFC 7540 (2015). Methods, status codes, and most headers stay as in HTTP/1.1, but the server may send objects by client priority, push unrequested objects, and interleave frames so a large object does not block small ones. A single TCP connection still stalls every object on packet loss.

nodes.label: HTTP/3
nodes.rationale: Adds security and per-object error and congestion control over UDP, so loss on one object does not stall the others the way HTTP/2 over one TCP connection does. Shown as HTTP/2 (slimmed) over QUIC over UDP.

nodes.label: QUIC
nodes.rationale: Quick UDP Internet Connections: application-layer protocol on UDP that establishes reliability, congestion control, authentication, and encryption in one RTT, versus serial TCP and TLS handshakes. A cached TLS session ticket allows a later 0-RTT handshake. Loss and congestion algorithms parallel TCP. Deployed on many Google servers and in Chrome and the mobile YouTube app.

nodes.label: HTTP head-of-line blocking
nodes.rationale: HTTP/1.1 pipelined GETs are answered in order, so a small object waits behind a large one, and TCP loss recovery stalls every object. That delay is why HTTP/2 divides objects into scheduled frames and why HTTP/3 moves per-object control off a single TCP connection.

nodes.label: SMTP
nodes.rationale: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol pushes mail over TCP port 25 from the sending mail server to the receiving server. Three phases: handshake (HELO), transfer (MAIL FROM, RCPT TO, DATA), closure (QUIT). Persistent connections, 7-bit ASCII, message ended by CRLF.CRLF. Unlike HTTP pull, SMTP is client push; multiple objects travel in one multipart message.

nodes.label: IMAP
nodes.rationale: Internet Mail Access Protocol retrieves, deletes, and folders mail that stays on the server. SMTP only delivers into the receiver mailbox. Webmail (Gmail, Hotmail, Yahoo) uses HTTP on top of SMTP to send and IMAP or POP to retrieve.

nodes.label: Mail user agent
nodes.rationale: Mail reader (for example Outlook or an iPhone mail client) composes, edits, and reads messages. Outgoing and incoming mail is stored on the server.

nodes.label: Mail server
nodes.rationale: Holds the user mailbox and a queue of outgoing messages. The sending server is the SMTP client; the receiving server is the SMTP server.

nodes.label: E-mail message format (RFC 2822)
nodes.rationale: RFC 2822 defines the message syntax (header lines To, From, Subject, then a blank line and ASCII body), distinct from SMTP envelope commands MAIL FROM and RCPT TO. Compared with HTML defining web documents while HTTP carries them.

nodes.label: Domain Name System (DNS)
nodes.rationale: Distributed hierarchical database and application-layer protocol mapping names and IP addresses. Also host aliasing, mail-server aliasing, and load distribution across replicated servers. A centralized DNS would be a single point of failure, a traffic bottleneck, distant, and hard to maintain. Comcast DNS about 600 billion queries/day; Akamai DNS about 2.2 trillion/day.

nodes.label: Root DNS servers
nodes.rationale: Contact of last resort when a name server cannot resolve a name. Thirteen logical root servers, each replicated many times. The Internet could not function without them.

nodes.label: Top-level domain DNS servers
nodes.rationale: Responsible for .com, .org, .net, .edu, and country domains. Network Solutions is the registry for .com and .net; Educause for .edu. Bombarding TLD servers is described as more dangerous than root DDoS because local caches often bypass the root.

nodes.label: Authoritative DNS servers
nodes.rationale: Organization or provider servers that hold the authoritative hostname-to-IP mappings for that organization's hosts. A registrar inserts NS and A records into the TLD so resolvers can find them.

nodes.label: Local DNS name server
nodes.rationale: Host queries go first to the ISP local DNS server, which answers from cache or forwards into the hierarchy. It does not strictly belong to the hierarchy. Find it with scutil --dns on macOS or ipconfig /all on Windows.

nodes.label: Iterated DNS query
nodes.rationale: The contacted server does not resolve the name itself. It replies with the next server to ask: I do not know this name, but ask this server. Illustrated for engineering.nyu.edu resolving gaia.cs.umass.edu via local, root, TLD, and authoritative servers.

nodes.label: Recursive DNS query
nodes.rationale: Puts the burden of resolution on the contacted name server, which queries further servers itself. That can place heavy load on upper levels of the hierarchy.

nodes.label: DNS caching
nodes.rationale: Any name server may cache a mapping and answer immediately. Entries expire after a TTL. TLD servers are typically cached locally, which also lets resolvers bypass the root. Cached data can be stale until all TTLs expire, so translation is best-effort.

nodes.label: DNS resource records
nodes.rationale: RR format is (name, value, type, ttl). A maps a hostname to an IP address. NS names the authoritative server for a domain. CNAME maps an alias to a canonical name. MX names the SMTP server for a name. Query and reply messages share one format with identification, flags (recursion desired/available, authoritative), and question, answer, authority, and additional sections.

nodes.label: DNSSEC
nodes.rationale: Provides authentication and message integrity for DNS. Counters spoofed replies and cache poisoning (RFC 4033). Root DDoS has not succeeded to date because of filtering and because local servers cache TLD addresses.

nodes.label: DASH
nodes.rationale: Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP. Server stores the video as chunks at several rates, replicated on CDN nodes, and a manifest lists their URLs. The client estimates bandwidth and chooses rate, timing, and server so the buffer neither starves nor overflows. Streaming video is described as encoding plus DASH plus playout buffering.

nodes.label: Content distribution network
nodes.rationale: A single mega-server does not scale: it is a single point of failure, a congestion point, and a long path to distant clients. A CDN stores copies at many sites. Enter-deep pushes servers into access networks (Akamai). Bring-home uses fewer larger clusters in POPs (Limelight). OTT operation must choose which node stores content and which node and rate serve a request.

nodes.label: Client playout buffering
nodes.rationale: Stored video has a continuous playout constraint, but network delay varies (jitter). A client buffer and playout delay absorb that jitter so playout timing can match the original timing. Pause, seek, and loss/retransmission remain separate challenges.

nodes.label: Video coding (CBR, VBR, MPEG)
nodes.rationale: Video is a constant-rate image sequence. Spatial coding removes redundancy inside a frame; temporal coding sends differences between frames. CBR keeps a fixed encoding rate; VBR changes with the amount of redundancy. Examples: MPEG-1 about 1.5 Mbps, MPEG-2 about 3-6 Mbps, MPEG-4 about 64 Kbps-12 Mbps on the Internet.

nodes.label: Akamai
nodes.rationale: Enter-deep CDN example: about 240,000 servers in more than 120 countries (2015). Also cited for DNS query volume of about 2.2 trillion queries per day.

nodes.label: Netflix Open Connect
nodes.rationale: Netflix stores copies of titles at worldwide Open Connect CDN nodes. The client uses a manifest to fetch the highest supportable rate and may switch rate or copy if the path is congested. A case study separates registration and accounting (Amazon cloud) from manifest retrieval and DASH streaming from CDN servers. With YouTube and Amazon Prime, cited as about 80% of residential ISP traffic in 2020.

nodes.label: FTP
nodes.rationale: File transfer application that requires no data loss, elastic throughput, and is not time sensitive. Runs over TCP. Cited as RFC 959 and as a client-server example.

nodes.label: RFC 5321
nodes.rationale: Cited as the SMTP specification.

nodes.label: RFC 7540
nodes.rationale: Cited as the 2015 HTTP/2 specification.

nodes.label: RFC 3501
nodes.rationale: Cited as the IMAP specification.

nodes.label: RFC 4033
nodes.rationale: Cited for DNSSEC authentication services.

nodes.label: RFC 2822
nodes.rationale: Cited as the syntax of the e-mail message itself, as distinct from the SMTP transfer protocol.

nodes.label: RFC 7230 and RFC 9110
nodes.rationale: Cited together as the HTTP specifications for Web documents. RFC 7231 is also named as defining HTTP, analogous to RFC 5321 for SMTP.

nodes.label: RFC 959
nodes.rationale: Cited as the FTP specification.

nodes.label: ICANN
nodes.rationale: Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers manages the root DNS domain.

nodes.label: Socket timeout (settimeout)
nodes.rationale: A process may wait on a socket reply or a timer. Python socket.settimeout arms blocking recv; if no segment arrives, recv raises a timeout exception caught by try/except. settimeout(None) clears it; settimeout(0) makes the socket non-blocking. Introduced so students practice timers before a later reliable-data-transfer assignment. select or multithreading can wait on several sockets.

nodes.label: GDPR and cookie identifiers
nodes.rationale: GDPR recital 30 (May 2018) treats online identifiers such as IP addresses and cookie IDs as capable of profiling natural persons. When cookies identify an individual they are personal data, and the user has explicit control over whether cookies are allowed.
